newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK continues to dominate global fund portfolios.
newsitem.headline: HK continues to dominate global fund portfolios.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks continue to dominate international portfolios, with LGT Asset Management revealing a 29 percent weighting in its global balanced fund during an investment seminar in Hong Kong on Monday.
"We are still confident we will be able to show further returns," said Lawrence Yip, senior portfolio manager at LGT, a unit of Liechtenstein Global Trust AG.

LGT, which manages US$80 billion in assets, said other key weightings in its global balanced fund were 10 percent Asia ex-Japan, 3.5 percent Japan, 12 percent United States, 20.5 percent Europe and 16 percent global bonds.
Hong Kong, Malaysia and the Philippines will continue to outperform the other Asian markets, Yip said. But he warned that increasing selectivity will be required to maintain performance in Hong Kong.
"Key sectors within the markets also diverged quite widely," Yip said. "In Hong Kong, property stocks had a bonanza while the utility sector languished."
Property stocks will continue to do well, partly because Hong Kong's property market is a cartel dominated by a handful of players capable of participating in a capital-intensive business, Yip said.
"The situation is not likely to change much in the next two to three years," he said.
"The big five local property conglomerates all have sizeable landbanks and do not appear in any danger of coming under threat from new entrants to the market."

Yip denied following other Asian asset managers who have shifted some Hong Kong weighting in Asia ex-Japan portfolios into Indonesia and Singapore. His weighting remains steady at about 40 percent, he said.
In general, Asia will benefit from a bottoming out of the U.S. inventory correction, with the first signs of increased volumes in electronics goods surfacing even though prices remain depressed.

LGT's favoured region in 1997 appears to be Europe, which chief economist John Greenwood expects to enjoy a year of rapid expansion thanks to easier money conditions and a convergence of bond yields ahead of the European Monetary Union.
"There has been a massive ease in monetary policy in many European countries," Greenwood said. "The result will be faster than consensus economic growth in Europe in 1997."
The United States, by contrast, is in an almost ideal "steady state" condition, with real gross domestic product rising at about 2.5 percent and the consumer price index at about three percent.
"The fairly flat yield curve suggests growth is unlikely to accelerate in 1997, and five to six percent growth of M2 and M3 support the case for continued low inflation," Greenwood said.

LGT is forecasting little change in U.S. rates, but said a 25-basis point cut later this year is possible if economic growth slips. A decline in the benchmark 30-year U.S. bond yield below six percent is also considered possible.

In Japan, another year of sub-par growth is forecast against a background of slow money, an overvalued yen and a lack of political leadership necessary to embark on aggressive deregulation and restructuring, Greenwood said.
"The Bank of Japan's low interest rates have not translated into faster money growth," he said.
LGT, which reduced its global balance fund weighting to 3.5 percent Japan from 13 percent in the first quarter of 1996, expects to remain underweight for the forseeable future.
